# Summary

H3 is a hierarchical hexagonal grid covering the globe.
Given a global random seed and an H3 resolution, every H3 cell on Earth gets assigned a unique sort index.
Selecting cells in the order of this index results in a spatially balanced sample.
The `sbsampling` package calculates both the grid and these sort indices mathematically on the fly.
This allows you to draw reproducible GRTS samples from hundreds of millions of spatial locations, without exceeding your computer's RAM or requiring heavy databases.

# The H3 discrete global grid system

The [H3](https://h3geo.org/) discrete global grid system is a geospatial indexing system developed at Uber to efficiently map latitude-longitude coordinates to discrete cells anywhere on Earth.

H3 is a hierarchical tessellation based on a hexagonal grid.
At its lowest resolution (Resolution 0), H3 tiles the Earth into 122 base cells: 110 hexagons and 12 pentagons.
The pentagons are necessary because a perfect sphere cannot be tiled using exclusively hexagons.
To minimize distortion for spatial analysis, the grid is specifically oriented so that all 12 pentagons fall entirely within the oceans.

H3 provides 15 additional [resolutions](https://h3geo.org/docs/core-library/restable/) of increasing precision, with the highest resolution cells covering approximately 1 m². The hierarchical tiling results in strict parent-child relationships, which are encoded directly into the cell's ID number.
Every parent hexagon cell has seven hexagon children.
Thus, when moving from resolution $k$ to $k+1$, the cell area will be approximately seven times smaller.

The H3 grid is a pure mathematical coordinate system.
Converting a GPS coordinate into an H3 cell, finding a cell's parent, or locating its neighbours involves no database lookups. 
It is calculated purely on the fly using spherical geometry and bitwise mathematics.

# The Generalised Random Tesselation Stratified algorithm (GRTS) and reverse hierarchical ordering

GRTS is an algorithm developed by Stevens and Olsen (2004) to generate spatially balanced probability samples.

If we drew a Simple Random Sample (SRS) of grid cells across a landscape, sample-to-sample variance would be high because with SRS some regions would be oversampled, while others would be empty.

Instead of randomly selecting individual cells, GRTS achieves spatial balance by shuffling the branches of the spatial tree.
When the algorithm looks at a parent cell and its 7 children, it randomly shuffles the order in which those children are visited.
This (re-)ordering can be seen as a mapping from space to a 1D line along which samples can be selected.

# Reverse hierarchical ordering: spreading the sample

If we read the shuffled tree from the top down (e.g., Base Cell &rarr; Resolution 1 &rarr; Resolution 2), consecutive cells in the 1D line would still be physically right next to each other inside the same parent hexagon and a systematic sample along the 1D line would be needed to achieve a well spread sample.

A better approach, is to use reverse hierarchical ordering.
When building the final sort index for a cell, the algorithm flips the importance of the hierarchy.
Instead of putting the top-level parent first, it puts the finest resolution child index first.
Because the hierarchy is reversed, consecutive numbers in the final sorted list come from completely different parent cells.
This reverse ordering forces the sequential sample to "jump" across the entire study area, filling in the landscape as evenly and sparsely as possible before ever returning to sample near a previously selected location.
This is a property that makes the algorithm suitable for master sampling applications or to easily select replacement samples.

## Converting an H3 cell index into a GRTS sort index

To calculate the GRTS sort key for any given cell, the algorithm climbs the H3 hierarchy to find the cell's parents at every resolution.
At each level, it uses a random number generator seeded by a combination of two variables:

-   **The `parent_id`**: By seeding the generator with the parent cell's unique ID, we guarantee that all 7 children of that parent will always be shuffled in the exact same order.

-   **The `global_seed`**: If we only used the parent ID, the sample would be locked into a single configuration. Adding the user-provided global seed to the shuffle allows us to draw an infinite number of statistically independent random samples.

Because this process for a single H3 cell index is a small, deterministic (conditional on the chosen global seed and H3 resolution) mathematical calculation, it can be executed entirely in the CPU cache, streaming H3 cells at high speed.
This completely bypasses the need for massive RAM allocations or large database files on disk.

If two researchers run `grts_h3()` on overlapping but different study areas using the same seed, the cells in the overlapping region will receive the exact same sort keys in both studies, ensuring perfect reproducibility with a zero-storage footprint.

## Example: from H3 cell to GRTS sort index

To make this concrete, let's walk through exactly how an H3 cell is unpacked into its geometric address, randomized, and repacked into a GRTS sort key.
We will use the official [H3 bit layout](https://h3geo.org/docs/core-library/h3Indexing/#bit-layout-of-h3index) to decode the index.

### Decoding the H3 hexadecimal string

Imagine we are drawing a sample at **Resolution 3**, and the engine encounters the H3 index `"832830fffffffff"`. 

This string is the canonical hexadecimal representation of a 64-bit integer (`u64`).
Because H3 drops leading zeros, the full 16-character string is actually `0832830fffffffff`.
If we convert this hexadecimal into its binary bit layout (`0000 1000 0011 0010 1000 0011 0000 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111`), we can read the exact geographic address of the cell:

* **Bits 63-52 (`0 0001 000 0011`):** Contains a reserved code (`0`), the mode (`0001`), a mode-dependent section (`000`) and the resolution (`0011`). It tells us this is a standard cell (Mode 1) at Resolution 3.
* **Bits 51-45 (`0010100`):** This 7-bit block equals **20**. The cell sits inside **Base Cell 20**.
* **Bits 44-42 (`000`):** The 3-bit child digit for Resolution 1 is **0**.
* **Bits 41-39 (`110`):** The 3-bit child digit for Resolution 2 is **6**.
* **Bits 38-36 (`000`):** The 3-bit child digit for Resolution 3 is **0**.
* **Bits 35-0 (`fffffffff`):** The remaining 12 x 3 = 36 bits are unused (Resolutions 4-15), so they are intentionally set to 1s.

So, our cell's true geometric address is: **Base Cell 20 &rarr; Child 0 &rarr; Child 6 &rarr; Child 0**.

### The GRTS shuffle (mathematical permutation)

To achieve spatial balance, we need to randomly shuffle this entire path. The algorithm calculates a deterministic random shuffle at every level of the spatial tree:

* **Resolution 0 (The Global Base Cells):** First, the 122 H3 base cells themselves are globally shuffled. 
  * Let's say our global permutation remaps Base Cell 20 to **85**.
* **Resolution 1:** The engine uses the parent cell (Base Cell 20) and the global seed to calculate a shuffle for its 7 children.
  * *Calculated Shuffle:* `[5, 1, 6, 0, 4, 3, 2]`
  * Our cell was child `0`. In this new shuffled order, 0 maps to **5**.
* **Resolution 2:** The engine uses the parent at Resolution 1 to calculate the next shuffle.
  * Our cell was child `6`. Let's say the new permutation maps 6 to **3**.
* **Resolution 3:** The engine uses the parent at Resolution 2 to calculate the final shuffle.
  * Our cell was child `0`. Let's say the new permutation maps 0 to **1**.

Our cell's new, randomized address is: **Base 85 &rarr; Resolution 1: 5 &rarr; Resolution 2: 3 &rarr; Resolution 3: 1**.

### Reverse hierarchical bit packing

If we created a sorting number using the top-down order (Base Cell first), our sample would still be geographically clustered.
All cells within Base Cell 20 would remain grouped together numerically.

To force the sample to spread evenly across the study area, `sbsampling::grts_h3()` applies **reverse hierarchical ordering** directly at the bit level.
It packs the newly shuffled digits into a brand new 64-bit integer, but it builds it from the ground up:

* **Bits 0-6:** The newly shuffled Base Cell (`85`) is placed at the very bottom (the least significant bits).
* **Bits 7-9:** The Resolution 1 digit (`5`) is shifted above the base cell.
* **Bits 10-12:** The Resolution 2 digit (`3`) is shifted higher.
* **Bits 13-15:** The Resolution 3 target digit (`1`) is shifted to the highest, most significant bits of the sequence.
* **Bits 16-63:** The remaining resolutions were unused and are zero padded for the sort key to be valid.

This becomes:

```text
000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 001 011 101 1010101
\_____________________________________________________________/ \_/ \_/ \_/ \_____/
                 Unused Zeros (Bits 16-63)                       R3  R2  R1  Base
                                                                (1) (3) (5)  (85)
```

These 64-bit integers are typically represented in R as 16-character hexadecimal strings. Converted to hex, our sort key is: `"0000000000002ed5"`.

Lexicographical sorting will perfectly match the numeric order, provided the strings are strictly zero-padded to a fixed length (e.g., keeping all 16 characters in the hexadecimal string `"0000000000002ed5"`).

By pushing the finest resolution digits into the higher bits and burying the base cell at the bottom, we have implemented a reverse hierarchical sort.

# Accounting for cell area differences

While H3 strives for uniformity, the cells are not perfect equal-area hexagons everywhere on the globe; cells introduce slight area distortions depending on their location on the sphere.
For a given resolution, cell areas can differ by a factor of two - in practice, this will often be much smaller if the region of interest is restricted (say, a country).

For statistical inference, we can either take the varying cell areas into account at the estimation stage or at the sample selection stage.
For the latter approach, `sbsampling::grts_h3()` has an argument `area_correction`.
When set to `TRUE`, it adjusts the inclusion probabilities of the cells so that they are sampled with probability proportional to their size (PPS).
An efficient Order Sampling technique (similar to Sequential Poisson Sampling) is used (Rosén 1997, Ohlsson 1998).
For each cell, the algorithm divides its spatially balanced GRTS sort key (which acts as a uniform random variable) by its true physical area to calculate an "effective key".
By selecting the $n$ cells with the smallest effective keys, the algorithm naturally scales the inclusion probabilities.
This ensures that larger cells are proportionately more likely to be selected, all while strictly maintaining the requested sample size and the spatial balance of the GRTS design.

# References

Rosén B. (1997). On sampling with probability proportional to size. Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference 62 (2): 159-191. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0378-3758(96)00186-3.

Ohlsson, E. (1998). Sequential Poisson Sampling. Journal of Official Statistics, 14(2), 149-162.

Stevens, D. L., & Olsen, A. R. (2004). Spatially Balanced Sampling of Natural Resources. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 99(465), 262–278. https://doi.org/10.1198/016214504000000250
